description: We're Kernel Panic Squad, a team of backend and automation engineers. We build real-time monitoring systems, APIs and dashboards (Python, FastAPI, Docker, Grafana), and we want to apply that to astronaut health: turning sensor data into live insights and early-warning alerts. Looking for teammates with skills in frontend (React/Vue), data science/ML, UI/UX design, or biomedical knowledge. Let's build something NASA-worthy!
summary: Far from Earth, astronauts have to judge their own health. Own Your Baseline is an offline-first health companion that learns each astronaut's own baseline from passive data and a 30-second check-in, flags drift in plain words with one next step, and says when to contact the flight surgeon. A clickable body map on NASA's EMU astronaut model covers the six indicators named in the challenge (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood), with trend charts and status shown by color, shape and word. Our difference is an open record: the flight surgeon sees the full record, the astronaut sees everything ground sees, and questions travel as a consult brief across a link delay of up to 20 minutes at Mars distance. Decision support, not a diagnosis. Demo vitals are simulated and labeled.
details:
What it does

- Visual self-assessment: a clickable 3D body map on NASA's EMU astronaut model, plus a 2D view that needs no WebGL. Six indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood), trend charts against the personal baseline, and status shown by color, shape and word.

- A 30-second morning check-in. Heart rate and sleep come from the wearable and are never typed.

- Drift alerts in three parts: what changed, one next step, and when to contact the flight surgeon.

- Cabin Link: cabin CO2 shown next to reported headaches, as a pattern to check, not a cause.

- Open record: the flight surgeon sees the full record, and the astronaut sees everything ground sees, including notes. Every sync is listed in a log the astronaut can read.

- Consult brief: the astronaut asks ground a question with the related items pinned. The reply comes back as advice, not an order.

- Ground link at station, Moon or Mars distance: queued items visibly travel, with a clock in real signal time (up to 20 minutes one way at Mars, per NASA HRP).

- Mission replay: scrub the mission day by day; the body map, cabin CO2, headaches, sleep and heart rate move under one playhead.

- Ask my record: plain-words answers about your own data that cite days and values and highlight them on the charts.

- Crew readiness for the commander (a level and a reason, no raw medical data), an environment switcher (station, spacecraft, rover, surface base) and a check-in streak.

How it works

- Personal baseline: 7 days of calibration, then each reading is compared with the astronaut's own band. NASA OSD-569 Earth reference ranges are shown beside it as reference only and never trigger an alert.

- One record feeds both views, so the astronaut and the flight surgeon always see the same picture. The ground link is simulated with queues, the way a delayed link works.

- The record assistant only restates facts the app already computed. It cannot change a status and is not sent crew names. Strong symptoms and medicine questions get a fixed "contact the flight surgeon" answer. Without a model key it answers by fixed rules, so the app works fully offline.

- Every threshold carries a citation or is labeled "Demo parameter".

Tools

React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js and d3 (web app); FastAPI, Pydantic and SQLite (API); VictoriaMetrics with a Python simulator and OSD-569 ETL (time series); Docker Compose. Design tokens from the NASA Horizon Design System, NASA Open MCT and Astro UXDS.

Goals

Give an astronaut far from Earth a tool that knows their own normal, explains drift in plain words, and turns a slow link to ground into one precise question. Next steps: real wearable data, an on-board assistant that needs no link, and clinician review of every threshold.
